findings.description: The inline policy grants full administrative control over ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:* and cloudwatch:* on Resource "*", violating least privilege. Compromise of this user's credentials would allow full data access in S3, arbitrary compute provisioning in EC2, and code execution/modification via Lambda across the entire account. The lambda:* and ec2:* grants also create a privilege escalation path (e.g. passing or attaching more privileged roles to Lambda functions or instances).

A static IAM access key is generated for a highly privileged user with no pgp_key set, so the secret access key is stored unencrypted in the Terraform state file (the encrypted_secret attribute will be empty without a PGP key). Anyone with read access to state obtains permanent credentials with the wildcard EC2/S3/Lambda/CloudWatch permissions attached to this user; long-lived keys also lack the automatic rotation of IAM role credentials.

The access key secret is exported as a root-level Terraform output without sensitive = true, so it is printed to the console and CI/CD logs on every apply and is readable via `terraform output`, leaking credential material for the over-privileged IAM user. The companion output.username further identifies the account to attack.
